coherence.reasons: Both run the same clean chain: bridge, why the draft plan fails, sized levers, sequencing, risks, asks. X's storyline is tighter, and its governing thought (3% is reachable) matches its 3.16% bridge. But that bridge leaves out the known 2027 wage step, which reappears on the risks slide and needs contingency levers to hold 3%. X's summary also quotes a one-time cost of up to $17.5M while asking for $10M, and one slide title is only a metric label. Y's governing thought is more precise (2.6% firm, second wave closes the gap) and its sections and appendix reconcile. But two of Y's titles say the plan "gets back to" or "reaches" 3.0% when the firm levers reach only 2.6%, and its self-invented starting hypothesis adds a layer. These tensions are of similar size.

judgment.reasons: Both reject the 8% cut and recommend essentially the same seven-lever plan, with delivery repriced rather than frozen or killed and the three long-lease stores deferred to a board vote. Y weighs alternatives and trade-offs better. It compares three options, including click-and-collect-only as a fallback that needs the owners' consent, and it also rejects deeper promotions and exiting all nine stores now. It builds the 2027 wage step and delivery rate rise into the baseline, so it admits the firm levers reach only about 2.6% and sizes a second wave with a mid-FY2027 trigger. It haircuts the promotion reset by 25% for lost traffic, nets the cost of reinvested hours against the shrink gain, gives low/base/high ranges, and itemises one-time costs. X's 3.2% rests on unhaircut promotion savings with traffic risk "unsized" and treats the wage step as a risk covered by contingency levers. One of those is "pass through in prices", despite the worsening price perception. X's contingency logic is sound but less rigorous.

evidence.reasons: Both reproduce the core numbers correctly: the margin bridge, the gross-margin decomposition (−0.70, −0.50, +0.18), the −$10.4M e-commerce drag, per-order losses of −$12.34 and −$1.64, the fee test at about $2.5M before the rate rise, and store exits at $6.6M and $4.4M. Y uses the critical evidence more fully. It splits labor into a wage effect (+1.11 pts) and a productivity offset (−0.77 pts) and notes total hours were roughly flat. It shows the e-commerce team's 6.1% turns to −0.4% on delivery cost alone, gives break-even incrementality (94% for delivery, 39% for click-and-collect), and shows delivery still loses about $9 an order after repricing. It tests the "promotions work" claim quantitatively while flagging it as correlation, and labels the shrink quartile data as correlation needing a pilot. X says "Harlow has already cut hours 6%", when it was hours per $1,000 of sales that fell. Its shrink leak of up to $10M attributes the whole shrink rise to labor, though it caveats this as an upper bound. X also lists the promotion cut among high-confidence levers on one slide and medium on another. Y's weak spots are a speculative −5% delivery contract target and a somewhat loose promotion break-even inference; both are bounded by ranges or caveats.

revision.reasons: Both correctly revise management's hypothesis: labor is about 13% of the decline, the 8% cut risks shrink, and the freeze locks in a loss. Both keep a targeted labor lever of about 3% in high-labor stores. Y handles the hypothesis more carefully. It quantifies what is true in management's view (wages alone would have added 1.11 pts) and what offset it. It explains why the dollar view misleads, carries the 2027 wage step into the baseline rather than dismissing wages, and flags the $14.5M saving as gross of shrink and service effects. It also tests its own replacement hypothesis against seven conditions and revises it, concluding that promotions and delivery alone are not enough. X's revision is correct and well evidenced but less nuanced, and it overstates the past hours cut.

overall.reasons: Both are strong, defensible answers of the key's preferred type, with a quantified bridge, sized levers that add up, and the covenant in view. X is more concise and gives a cleaner headline. Y would serve the CEO better in front of a board and a lender. It is candid that the firm levers reach about 2.6% once known headwinds are counted, and it offers a prepared second wave and a fallback option. It haircuts for traffic loss, gives ranges and sensitivities with triggers, itemises the one-time budget, and warns that covenant headroom disappears if erosion continues. X's more optimistic 3.2% depends on leaving the wage step outside the base and on unhaircut gross-margin levers.
